question: Milk prices have recently risen significantly throughout the world. One of the main drivers of this price increase is the growing demand for Chinese dairy products when these are in short supply and local production is in decline. As a result, milk prices have continued to increase worldwide since September, following quite substantial decreases in May.

For a third time running, prices of dairy products at the New Zealand Global Dairy Trade (GDT) auction have risen steeply. Recent data from the 3 October auction show that the price index for dairy products marketed rose by 4.4% over mid-September. The price of skimmed milk powder has jumped up, and now stands at over EUR 2 400 per tonne. At the same time, the price of butter has increased by 1.

3% to EUR 4 591/tonne, while that of cheddar decreased by 4.8 %. In view of the increase in prices of milk and dairy products and the factors behind this increase, what tools can the European Commission use to protect European consumers against these price rises?
answer: As announced in its communication on Food Security of March 2022 (1), the Commission took different initiatives to reduce the effects of the price surge on consumers, e.g., through improved flexibility of the Fund for European Aid to the Most Deprived, or through the Temporary Crisis and Transition Framework for State Aid, which allows Member States to use EU State aid rules to tackle the spike of energy prices (2).

The Commission also welcomed national initiatives to support consumers, including the possibility of applying reduced VAT (value-added tax) rates on essential food (3) or providing food vouchers to the most vulnerable.

The EU continues monitoring the proper functioning of the internal market to ensure it works for the benefit of both farmers and consumers and works with national competition authorities to identify anti-competitive practices that may inflate food prices.
